'''John Henry Coates''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}}<ref name="royal">{{cite web|url=https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo==%27EC%2F1985%2F08%27) |title=EC/1985/08: Coates, John Henry |publisher=The Royal Society |archive-date=8 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190708073537/https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini |location=London |url-status=dead }}</ref> (26 January 1945 – 9 May 2022) was an Australian mathematician who was the [[Sadleirian professor of pure mathematics]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] in the United Kingdom from 1986 to 2012.<ref name="mathgene">{{MathGenealogy|id=20324}}</ref><ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor Biography|id=Coates}}</ref><ref name="emma">{{Cite web |url=http://www.emma.cam.ac.uk/about/fellows/display/index.cfm?fellow=83 |title=Emmanuel College profile: Professor John Coates |access-date=17 November 2007 |archive-date=29 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120829200305/http://www.emma.cam.ac.uk/about/fellows/display/index.cfm?fellow=83 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Macfarlane interview">{{Cite web |url=https://www.sms.cam.ac.uk/media/1114747 |title=interviewed by Alan Macfarlane 25 February 2008 (video) |access-date=13 August 2019 |archive-date=6 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506040441/https://www.sms.cam.ac.uk/media/1114747 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="scopus">{{Scopus|id= 7101947985}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1007/s10240-004-0029-3| title = The GL2 Main Conjecture for Elliptic Curves without Complex Multiplication| journal = Publications mathématiques de l'IHÉS| volume = 101| pages = 163–208| year = 2005| last1 = Coates | first1 = J. | last2 = Fukaya | first2 = T. | last3 = Kato | first3 = K. | last4 = Sujatha | first4 = R. | last5 = Venjakob | first5 = O. | arxiv = math/0404297| s2cid = 13996298}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Coates was born the son of J. H. Coates and B. L. Lee on 26 January 1945<ref name="ww">{{cite web |url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U11293 |title=COATES, Prof. John Henry |work=Who's Who 2014, A & C Black, an imprint of Bloomsbury Publishing plc, 2014; online edn, Oxford University Press |access-date=27 May 2014 |archive-date=10 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220510054401/https://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/10.1093/ww/9780199540884.001.0001/ww-9780199540884-e-11293;jsessionid=9A47D0FDDD9C52026CCA74D7150F442D |url-status=live }}{{subscription required}}</ref> and grew up in Possum Brush (near [[Taree]]) in [[New South Wales]], Australia.<ref name="Singh 2017 p. 215">{{cite book | last=Singh | first=S. | title=Fermat's Enigma: The Epic Quest to Solve the World's Greatest Mathematical Problem | publisher=Knopf Doubleday Publishing Group | year=2017 | isbn=978-0-525-43532-7 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xKDnDQAAQBAJ&pg=PT215 | access-date=10 May 2022 | page=215}}</ref> Coates Road in Possum Brush is named after the family farm on which he grew up.<ref>{{cite web|title=Whereis: Possum Brush|url=http://www.whereis.com/nsw/possum-brush#session=MTE=|access-date=5 March 2013|archive-date=30 June 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130630175220/http://www.whereis.com/nsw/possum-brush#session=MTE=|url-status=live}}</ref> Before university he spent a summer working for [[BHP]] in [[Newcastle, New South Wales]], though he was not successful in gaining a university scholarship with the company. Coates attended [[Australian National University]] on scholarship as one of the first undergraduates, from which he gained a BSc degree. He then moved to France, doing further study at the [[École normale supérieure (Paris)|École Normale Supérieure]] in Paris, before moving again, this time to England.<ref name="death" /><ref name="Macfarlane interview" />

==Career==
In England he did postgraduate research at the University of Cambridge, his doctoral dissertation being on [[P-adic number|''p''-adic]] analogues of [[Baker's theorem|Baker's method]]. In 1969, Coates was appointed assistant professor of mathematics at [[Harvard University]] in the United States, before moving again in 1972 to [[Stanford University]] where he became an associate professor.<ref name="death" />

In 1975, he returned to England, where he was made a [[fellow]] of [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge|Emmanuel College]],<ref name="KIT">{{cite web | title=Department of Mathematics – On the arithmetic of the Gross family of elliptic curves with complex multiplication | website=KIT | url=https://www.math.kit.edu/iag3/~januszewski/event/johncoates2018/en | access-date=10 May 2022}}</ref> and took up a lectureship. Here he supervised the PhD of [[Andrew Wiles]], and together they proved a partial case of the [[Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture]] for [[elliptic curve]]s with [[complex multiplication]].<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1007/bf01402975| title = On the conjecture of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer| journal = Inventiones Mathematicae| volume = 39| issue = 3| pages = 223| year = 1977| last1 = Coates | first1 = J.| last2 = Wiles | first2 = A.| bibcode = 1977InMat..39..223C| s2cid = 189832636}}</ref>

In 1977, Coates moved back to Australia, becoming a professor at the [[Australian National University]],<ref name="KIT" /> where he had been an undergraduate. The following year, he moved back to France, taking up a professorship at the [[Paris-Sud University|University of Paris XI]] at [[Orsay]]. In 1985, he returned to the École Normale Supérieure, this time as professor and director of mathematics.<ref name="death" />

From 1986 until his death, Coates worked in the [[Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge|Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics (DPMMS)]] of the University of Cambridge.<ref name="death" /> He was head of DPMMS from 1991 to 1997.<ref name="DPMMS">{{cite web |title=Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics {{!}} Welcome to DPMMS |url=https://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/ |website=University of Cambridge |access-date=10 May 2022 |quote=Professor John Coates (26th January 1945 to 9th May 2022) We are sad to learn of the death of John Coates FRS, Sadleirian Professor 1986-2012. John was a distinguished number theorist and a dynamic Head of DPMMS 1991-97. He was instrumental in shaping the current Department and in the establishment of the Kuwait Professorship and the Kuwait Foundation Lectures. }}</ref>

His research interests included [[Iwasawa theory]], number theory and arithmetical algebraic geometry.<ref name="death" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Professor John Coates |url=https://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/person/jhc13 |website=University of Cambridge |access-date=10 May 2022 |archive-date=7 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210707041608/https://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/person/jhc13 |url-status=live }}</ref>

He served on the Mathematical Sciences jury for the [[Infosys Prize]] in 2009.<ref>{{cite web |title=Infosys Prize 2009 |url=https://www.infosys-science-foundation.com/downloads/ISF-Booklet-2009.pdf |website=Infosys Science Foundation |access-date=10 May 2022 |page=13 |archive-date=9 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210909105712/https://www.infosys-science-foundation.com/downloads/ISF-Booklet-2009.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
Coates was elected a fellow of the [[Royal Society]] of London in 1985,<ref name="Royal Society 2019">{{cite web | title=John Coates | website=[[Royal Society]] | date=2 December 2019 | url=https://royalsociety.org/people/john-coates-11240/ | access-date=10 May 2022}}</ref> and was President of the [[London Mathematical Society]] from 1988 to 1990.<ref name="Maths History 1945">{{cite web | title=John Coates – Biography | website=Maths History | date=26 January 1945 | url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Coates/ | access-date=10 May 2022}}</ref> The latter organisation awarded him the [[Senior Whitehead Prize]] in 1997,<ref name="death" /> for "his fundamental research in number theory and for his many contributions to mathematical life both in the UK and internationally".<ref>{{cite journal |title=Records of Proceedings at Meetings |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |date=July 1998 |volume=30 |issue=4 |pages=442 |doi=10.1112/S0024609398004445|s2cid=247660423 }}</ref> His nomination for the Royal Society reads:

{{Cquote|Distinguished for his contributions to the theory of numbers, in particular to the study of transcendence, cyclotomic fields and elliptic curves. In addition to his own important contributions he has been a stimulating influence on colleagues and students. Together with his pupil A. Wiles he achieved the first major breakthrough towards a proof of the Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer conjectures.<ref name="royal" />}}

==Personal life and death==
Coates married Julie Turner in 1966, with whom he had three sons.<ref name="ww" /> He collected [[Japanese pottery and porcelain]].<ref name="Macfarlane interview" /> He died at his home in Cambridge, on 9 May 2022, at the age of 77.<ref name="death">{{Cite web |url=https://www.emma.cam.ac.uk/about/news/?id=577 |title=Emmanuel College website, retrieved 9 May 2022 |access-date=9 May 2022 |archive-date=10 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220510054400/https://www.emma.cam.ac.uk/about/news/?id=577 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="DPMMS" /><ref name="ODNB">{{cite web |title=Coates, John Henry |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/display/10.1093/odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-90000383190?rskey=idQRIA&result=56 |website=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |access-date=8 July 2026}}</ref>
